title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR erotemata 1–7 on head/imputation
pass_a_gloss: GAR's seven: (1) If he sinned as head of the race, why not also be punished under that title? (2) Why is Adam's sin imputed to posterity rather than posterity's to Adam? (3) Since he did not at once cease to be head after that sin, why are later sins not equally imputed? (4) Why impute the actual (a passing act) rather than the habitual (a lasting vice)? (5) If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not the first act of begetting—yet no one says we in Adam begot Cain or Seth? (6) If Adam's sin is ours by imputation as Christ's righteousness is, why is Christ called our righteousness but Adam not called our sin? (7) Is 'we sinned in Adam' proper or improper speech? Proper speech cannot say we both were and were not when Adam sinned; if improper, reduce it—and properly, being in Adam means drawing origin from him, or his being as remote cause of ours.
pass_b_english: GAR. 1. If he sinned as the head of the human race, why ought he not also to have been punished under that title? 2. Why is Adam's sin rather imputed to posterity than posterity's to Adam? 3. Since Adam after that sin did not at once cease to be head, why are Adam's following sins not equally imputed to posterity as the first? 4. Why is actual sin, which is a transient action, rather said to be imputed than habitual, which was a permanent vice? 5. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why not also the first act of begetting? Yet no one would say that we in Adam begot Cain or Seth. 6. If as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why is Christ called our righteousness, but Adam is not also called our sin? 7. When we are said to have sinned in Adam, is it proper or improper speech? It cannot be called proper unless we say that something simultaneously is and is not: for properly speaking, when Adam sinned, we would have been, we would not have been. If it is not proper, it must be reduced to the proper. But what does it properly signify that we were in Adam, except that we draw origin from Adam, or that Adam's being is the cause of our being?
source_text: GAR. 1. Si peccavit ut caput generis humani, cur non etiam puniri debuit eo nomine? 2. Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quam posterorum Adae imputatur? 3. Cum Adamus post illud peccatum, confestim non desierit esse caput, cur non sequentia Adami peccata aeque posteris imputantur atque primum? 4. Cur potius actuale peccatum, quod est actio transiens, imputari dicitur, quam habituale, quod fuit vitium permanens? 5. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturae, cur non etiam primus actus generandi? Nemo tamen dixerit nos in Adamo Cainum aut Sethum genuisse. 6. Si ut Christi justitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adae nostrum est imputatione, cur non, ut Christus dicitur, justitia nostra, dicitur etiam Adamus peccatum nostrum? 7. Cum dicimur peccasse in Adamo, estne propria, an impropria locutio? Propria dici non potest, nisi dicamus, aliquid simul esse & non esse: proprie enim loquendo, tum cum Adamus peccavit, fuissemus, non fuissemus. Si propria non est, revocanda est ad propriam. Quid autem significat proprie nos fuisse in Adamo, nisi nos ducere ab Adamo originem, vel esse Adami esse causam nostri esse?

choices.choice: Record GAR's seven head/imputation questions without yet answering
